1050.bp: Companies constantly decide which products to discount and by how much to maximize profit. If you offer too much discount, you lose money per sale. Too little, and customers buy from competitors instead. The real goal is figuring out the exact price cut that turns each customer into a buyer without leaving profit on the table.
1050.wh: Knowing how many extra sales a discount creates (the treatment effect) sounds like it should solve this—but it doesn't automatically tell you the right discount amount. Two very different discounts might create the same number of new buyers; the math of optimization requires something sharper: predicting the exact threshold price where each customer switches from 'no sale' to 'sale', which is a different prediction problem altogether.

Knowing how many extra sales a discount creates (the treatment effect) sounds like it should solve this—but it doesn't automatically tell you the right discount amount. Two very different discounts might create the same number of new buyers; the math of optimization requires something sharper: predicting the exact threshold price where each customer switches from 'no sale' to 'sale', which is a different prediction problem altogether.
1050.ap: The method works in two stages. First, it makes a rough guess at where each customer's price threshold lies by using a clever trick: sorting past purchase decisions to detect patterns, and noting that expected threshold prices are mathematically independent from observed actual purchases. Second, it fine-tunes these guesses by using an unequal penalty—penalizing certain kinds of mistakes more heavily than others—to lock in better estimates. Finally, it ranks candidates by their 'bang for buck' (Sharpe ratio) to pick which ones actually get the discount under a budget cap.
1050.ww: The independence trick works because what someone would have bought at different prices is not the same as what they did buy; this hidden threshold is separable from the noise in what we actually observed. The asymmetric penalty works because real-world costs are lopsided—leaving profitable customers unsubsidized hurts more than slightly overspending on price-insensitive ones—so penalizing mistakes differently mirrors the real economic stakes.
1050.po: In three public datasets and a live A/B test on a real platform, this method beats existing approaches, delivering measurably higher profit from subsidy allocation. It correctly predicts which customers need a discount and which price points flip them into buyers.

1051.bp: Computers need to find objects in images using only weak labels—for example, knowing a photo contains a 'bicycle' but not where it is in the frame. This is cheaper than manually drawing boxes around every object, but it tricks the algorithm into focusing on easy-to-spot textures (like a wheel rim) rather than understanding the whole thing (the complete bike frame).
1051.wh: Weak supervision breaks two ways: the model zones in on one distinctive part (part domination—seeing only the wheel) or blurs the object's edges into the background (merged detection—seeing wheel plus tablecloth as one blob). Both stem from the same root: the model never learns that an object is made of parts that fit together in a specific way.
1051.ap: The method builds up from parts to wholes, mimicking how humans see. It creates a dictionary of 'semantic parts' (wheel, seat, handlebars, chain) using large language models as a guide. It then trains smaller detectors to recognize each part in isolation by finding consistent patterns across many training images. Finally, it assembles these detected parts into complete objects, enforcing that parts only stick together in sensible configurations.
1051.ww: Teaching the model about structure works because parts are simpler to learn than whole objects—a wheel is a wheel whether it's on a racing bike or a cargo bike. Once the model knows what parts exist and how they connect, it can build complete objects, and it no longer gets fooled by stray textures that happen to share color or edge patterns.
1051.po: On standard benchmarks, this approach outperforms existing weak-supervision methods. More remarkably, it can detect new types of objects it has never seen—because instead of memorizing category names, it knows parts and how they combine, so it can generalize to any object describable by its components.

1052.bp: E-commerce sites want to know which customers will actually buy, not just which ones are interested. Someone might click, add to cart, read reviews—all signs of interest—but then abandon the purchase because of price, stock, or choice paralysis. These hesitant customers are different from ones who aren't interested at all, and treating them differently could convert more sales.
1052.wh: Most recommendation systems bin every non-purchase into one bucket: 'negative' or 'not interested'. But that conflates two different groups: people who actively disliked the product (true negatives) and people who wanted it but didn't complete the buy (hesitation). Mixing them corrupts the model's learning because it hides a large group of high-value opportunities.
1052.ap: The method learns to separate hesitation from disinterest using a two-part inference system. It first identifies successful conversions and learns what 'intent to buy' looks like from those cases. Then it applies that learned intent-detector to the abandoned cases, asking: 'If this customer had followed through, what would their intent signal have been?' This surfaces high-intent hesitators. To separate genuine hesitation from cases where customers switched to a competitor's item instead, it adds a penalty for competitor alternatives, sharpening the distinction.
1052.ww: This works because intent and final purchase are connected but distinct: many intent signals lead to purchase, but some don't (that's hesitation). By learning intent first and then spotting where intent exists without purchase, the model correctly identifies who wanted the item but stumbled before checkout. The competitor penalty works because one specific alternative temptation is different from general loss of interest.
1052.po: The framework accurately flags high-intent hesitators who can be re-engaged with targeted interventions like discounts or stock notifications. This lets platforms focus retention effort on customers most likely to convert, rather than wasting effort on truly uninterested users.

1053.bp: Searching for 3D scenes (architectural spaces, room layouts, outdoor environments) using natural language queries is difficult because text and 3D structure live in completely different worlds—one is sequential words, the other is spatial geometry. Currently, doing this well requires collecting and labeling thousands of matching text-scene pairs, which is expensive and brittle when queries or scene types are unfamiliar.
1053.wh: Existing approaches treat retrieval like learning a single joint space from paired examples, which requires massive labeled datasets and fails on novel scene types or open-vocabulary queries the system never trained on. The real blocker is the mismatch: text describes scenes abstractly and globally, while 3D data encodes spatial and visual specifics that don't translate directly.
1053.ap: Instead of forcing text and 3D into a shared space, the method converts both into a common textual representation. It reads the 3D scene (extracting what's there, how things relate, spatial layout) and describes it in natural language using large language models. The query stays as text. Both now speak the same language: plain descriptions compatible with off-the-shelf text embedding models. To handle complex scenes without breaking the LLM's coherence, it breaks scenes into 'roles' (foreground objects, spatial relations, materials) and builds each piece separately. For matching, it uses a structured alignment strategy: instead of comparing whole descriptions, it homes in on the relevant part of the query and aligns it locally against matching pieces of the scene description.
1053.ww: Text-to-text comparison is far more stable and generalizable than text-to-3D gaps, because large language models have already learned rich structure from vast amounts of text. Converting 3D to text leverages this learned structure. The local alignment works because queries are often about specific spatial details or object relations; pinpointing those in the scene description before comparing reduces noise from irrelevant scene context.
1053.po: The method retrieves correct 3D scenes from queries without any paired training data. It beats both systems trained on large labeled datasets and other zero-shot baselines, and it generalizes robustly to unfamiliar scene distributions and open-vocabulary queries.

1054.bp: Movie or music recommendations rely on collaborative filtering: the insight that if Alice and Bob rated the same movies similarly before, Bob's unrated movies are probably good recommendations for Alice. The simplest versions (comparing users based on how similar their past ratings are) often work better in practice than complex deep-learning models, yet they're fundamentally limited to comparing immediate neighbors, missing bigger patterns.
1054.wh: A similarity-based recommender only looks one step away: 'users who are similar to me'. But it misses patterns like 'a group of friends who collectively love indie films' or 'users three degrees away who share niche tastes'. Computing similarity at group-level or across multi-step paths is combinatorially explosive—there are too many possible combinations to check them all.
1054.ap: The method extends similarity-based methods to groups and multi-hop connections while keeping computation feasible. It uses MinHash, a probabilistic technique for quickly estimating set overlaps: instead of actually checking all possible pairs in a group or path, MinHash gives a fast approximate answer. This lets the model capture how similar a user is to different groups of friends, or how their tastes align with friends-of-friends, without the exponential blowup in compute that exact calculation would require.
1054.ww: MinHash works by hashing items to signatures that preserve overlap information—if two sets share many items, their hashes are likely similar. This approximation is loose enough to be fast yet tight enough to be useful for ranking. Extending similarity this way captures combinatorial patterns: a user might not match one friend closely, but match a trio of friends together, and that group signal is what drives good recommendations.
1054.po: On three public datasets, this extended similarity-based approach matches or beats state-of-the-art deep models while remaining interpretable and efficient. It demonstrates that the simplicity and transparency of similarity-based methods, when enhanced to see beyond immediate neighbors, is a competitive and practical alternative.

1055.bp: Finding communities in graphs—tight clusters of nodes with lots of internal connections—is useful everywhere: from detecting fraud rings to finding topic-specific user groups in social networks. Recent neural methods learn to recognize communities, but they require training on a specific graph and won't work on a new graph without retraining from scratch, which is expensive and slow.
1055.wh: Most neural models overfit to the specific structure of their training graphs. If the graph changes (different network topology, different neighborhood patterns), the model's learned features no longer match reality. The core problem is that real-world graphs vary wildly in their local density, connectivity direction, and whether nodes with strong ties have similar attributes or opposite ones—neural models trained on one don't transfer.
1055.ap: The method trains once on diverse source graphs and deploys directly to unseen graphs without retraining. It uses two key techniques. First, it aligns feature dimensions and semantics across domains using spectral analysis (which captures global structure properties) in a community-aware way, so a feature learned on one graph's community structure can map sensibly to another graph's structure. Second, it tokenizes both local and global structural context into a sequence and feeds it to a Transformer, then applies diffusion-based smoothing to adapt predictions when encountering unexpected graph properties on new data.
1055.ww: Spectral alignment works because global connectivity patterns (degree distribution, clustering tendency) are somewhat stable across graph domains, providing an anchor. The diffusion-based refinement works because it's a gentle process that doesn't require full retraining; it gradually pushes predictions toward consistency with local neighborhoods on the new graph, correcting drift without catastrophic forgetting.
1055.po: The framework successfully finds communities in entirely new graphs that it never trained on, with performance matching or beating retraining-based methods. This cuts deployment time dramatically and enables one trained model to be deployed across hundreds of different graph problems.

1056.bp: Large language models answer questions well when users know exactly what they want, but real queries are messy: vague, evolving, shaped by mental habits and biases ('I know AI is taking over' as a premise). The model guesses what the user really means and sometimes reinforces bad premises instead of correcting them. The real gap is that models don't model the user's mental state—what they know, what they're biased toward, how that shifts—so they can't personalize deeply.
1056.wh: Existing fixes ask clarifying questions iteratively, which helps narrow down intent but then defaults to generic responses. The problem is that understanding intent isn't enough; you also need to understand mental state: what prior beliefs is the user carrying? What are they biased toward? Does the user's thinking evolve as they interact? These stable but evolving mental patterns are invisible in standard interaction models.
1056.ap: The method builds a neural network model of the user's mental state as a three-layer graph, inspired by how neuroscientists model mentalizing in the human brain. It stores long-term mental states (beliefs, preferences) and updates them with each interaction. When a new query arrives, it uses a spreading activation algorithm (letting signal propagate through the mental graph with older beliefs decaying faster) to surface the most relevant mental context for that query. This context then gets encoded and injected into the language model via a lightweight adapter (LoRA), steering the model toward responses aligned with the user's actual mental state rather than generic answers.
1056.ww: The spreading activation mechanism works because mental states form networks: one belief connects to others, and understanding which beliefs are currently active requires spreading activation through those connections. Temporal decay is important because recent thoughts matter more than old ones. Injecting this context via LoRA works because it guides the language model without fully retraining, making the adaptation lightweight yet effective.
1056.po: The system generates personalized responses that reflect the user's actual mental model, beliefs, and evolving context, rather than generic answers. It tracks how the user's thinking changes across interactions, delivering truly personalized intent understanding that outperforms standard iterative clarification approaches.

1057.bp: People choose between search engines and AI chatbots for different reasons, and those choices reveal deeper differences in how they think about finding information. Understanding these differences is critical for designing better search tools: should your system emphasize finding authoritative sources or providing quick, polished summaries? The answer depends on what users actually expect and how they behave in different situations.
1057.wh: We don't have clear empirical data on when and why people pick one tool over another, how they actually use them (versus what they say they prefer), and how that varies by information need. People often say they value different things than they actually do—for example, claiming to value verification while trusting chatbot summaries on health questions.
1057.ap: Researchers surveyed 84 people about their actual recent experiences with both search engines and chatbots, asking about the types of tasks, what triggered each tool choice, what they found, and which tool they'd pick again. They categorized the patterns that emerged from analyzing these reports.
1057.ww: Real behavior often contradicts stated preferences because people have multiple goals in tension: wanting reliable sources but valuing speed, wanting authority but accepting personalized shortcuts when stakes feel low. Asking about actual recent interactions (not hypotheticals) captures this friction, revealing the real tradeoffs people make.
1057.po: The study found that people use search engines with a 'Browse and Verify' mindset—they gather multiple sources and check them—whereas they use chatbots with a 'Delegate and Consume' mindset—they trust the AI to summarize. However, people paradoxically turn to chatbots even for high-stakes decisions (health, relationships), suggesting tool choice depends on urgency and perceived authority, not just stated information-seeking philosophy. This misalignment points to design opportunities for tools that support reliable assessment and transparent sources.

1058.bp: Large internet companies operate multiple separate apps (video, reading, shopping, gaming), but users move between them and their interests cross over—someone who watches cooking videos might enjoy recipe articles and shop for kitchen gear. Current recommendation systems ignore these cross-domain interests, treating each app in isolation and missing valuable signals about what users actually care about across their life.
1058.wh: When a user's behavior sequence flows across apps, it's usually pooled together into simple summaries for efficiency, losing the rich pattern information. Different domains emphasize different features (one is text-heavy, another has images), so features don't line up neatly across domains. And existing methods don't model how the same user's intent changes depending on which domain they're in right now—sports interest might sway video recommendations but not book recommendations.
1058.ap: The system (STAR-CDR) builds cross-domain interest by threading three components together. First, it extracts cross-domain interest signals by keeping detailed behavior sequences and marking which domain and scenario each action came from, preserving fine-grained context. Second, it routes the signal through domain-specific expert components adaptively—different experts for video vs. reading—and recalibrates which experts activate based on the current scenario and task, so the same user's interest is expressed differently depending on context. Third, it aligns multimodal features (images, text, ID numbers) by using the cross-domain interest as a guide for gating, ensuring features from different domains are weighted appropriately.
1058.ww: Keeping detailed domain-scenario-task context works because user interest is truly different across contexts: someone might want trending viral videos but niche books in the same session. The adaptive routing works because it lets the system dynamically weight different expertise paths instead of forcing a one-size-fits-all model. Feature alignment through interest-guided gating works because it lets the system decide which modality matters for which domain (video needs strong visual features; reading emphasizes text), rather than forcing all domains into the same feature space.
1058.po: The system delivers recommendations that account for user interests that span apps—if someone engages with a certain type of content across multiple domains, that signal boosts relevant recommendations in each domain. Industrial deployment shows this captures cross-product collaboration and recommendation quality improvements over domain-isolated baselines.

1059.bp: Social media platforms struggle to detect automated bot accounts (fake engagement, misinformation distribution) because bots don't necessarily act like other bots—they're created to mimic different types of users. A good bot detector needs to spot when an account's behavior pattern doesn't match its stated or apparent type, which means understanding both the account itself and its neighbors in the network.
1059.wh: Existing neural methods assume that a user's friends reveal who they are—your neighbors predict your nature. But this breaks on Twitter-like platforms where people follow politicians they disagree with, celebrity fans follow strangers, and bot networks deliberately connect to diverse accounts to appear organic. In sparse, directed, and heterophilic graphs (where friends often differ from each other), this assumption fails catastrophically.
1059.ap: The detector explicitly models discrepancy between self and neighbors. It learns what each account is like from its own attributes (tweets, profile text, follower count) without assuming the network neighborhood confirms it. Then, it sends messages through the network using a bidirectional aggregation: one path for incoming interactions ('who follows me') and one for outgoing ('who I follow'), capturing asymmetric behavior separately. Crucially, it preserves the mismatch between self-representation and network signals instead of smoothing over it. If an account looks like a bot but has typical human neighbors, or vice versa, that discrepancy is the signal, not noise to eliminate.
1059.ww: Self-neighborhood discrepancy is diagnostic because bots often mask themselves—mimicking user behavior in attributes while maintaining network ties to other bots, or conversely, acting like humans but connected to bot networks. Capturing incoming vs. outgoing separately matters because bot networks often have asymmetric follow patterns (bots follow each other in coordinated ways). Preserving discrepancy works because over-smoothing the network signal erases the very patterns that distinguish bots.
1059.po: On multiple benchmark datasets, the detector consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. It is more effective at catching bots that hide in networks where a neighborhood assumption would fail, making it practically deployable on real social platforms with complex, sparse graphs.

1060.bp: AI systems answer complex multi-step questions by searching for documents, reading them, reasoning, then searching again (retrieval-augmented generation). The challenge is showing users *why* the answer is correct: what exact part of which document proved it? With text-only retrieval, this is vague—users get a document title and have to hunt through pages. With visual documents (slides, PDFs with charts), converting to plain text loses spatial reasoning and layout logic entirely.
1060.wh: Parsing documents into plain text creates two problems: users must manually locate evidence in lengthy documents, and visual reasoning is destroyed. Slides with diagrams, timelines, or spatial arrangements become meaningless text once converted. But most retrieval systems work with text only, so they can't leverage visual structure even when it's the key to understanding.
1060.ap: The system (Chain of Evidence) takes screenshots of retrieved documents and reasons over them directly using a vision-language model (Qwen-VL). Instead of parsing text, it keeps the visual layout intact. When the model identifies evidence for answering a query, it outputs a precise bounding box on the screenshot, showing exactly where the evidence is. This visual citation chains together: query → retrieved document → exact visual location → answer. It evaluates on both web pages (structured layouts) and presentation slides (complex diagrams).
1060.ww: Vision-language models trained on large multimodal datasets understand both text and spatial layout, so they can reason over documents as humans do—seeing a chart's title, axes, and data simultaneously. Bounding boxes are more precise than text citations because they pinpoint the exact visual region, and they preserve all context including diagrams, colors, and layout that make the evidence obvious to humans.
1060.po: The system retrieves evidence with precise pixel-level attribution, eliminating manual document hunting. On web pages and especially on complex slides with diagrams, fine-tuned Qwen-VL significantly outperforms text-based retrieval, capturing visual semantic content that text conversion discards. Users see exactly which part of a document proves the answer.

1061.bp: Video search systems retrieve clips matching natural language descriptions—'show me a dog running in the park'—but they typically assume the clip *exists* in the video. In reality, sometimes the queried moment isn't there, or the user's phrased query implies something incorrect ('the robot dancing' when it's actually a person). A robust retrieval system needs to refuse bad queries instead of hallucinating false matches.
1061.wh: Simply retrieving the best-matching moment assumes the query is answerable, which fails in two realistic ways. First, similar but irrelevant moments interfere—a cat running looks similar to a dog running, so the model gets confused. Second, once the model makes a wrong decision (retrieving an irrelevant moment), that mistake affects future reasoning in unrecoverable ways, because the system can't backtrack and reconsider.
1061.ap: The system (ARROW) learns to detect and resist interference using an adversarial approach. It has two parts: a Gradient-induced Semantic Adversary that actively probes the model by amplifying exactly the kind of semantic confusion that trips it up (similar-but-wrong moments), and an Adversarial Reliability Predictor that observes how the model behaves under this pressure and assigns confidence scores to its decisions. High confidence means the decision is stable under interference; low confidence flags unreliable predictions that should be rejected.
1061.ww: Testing under adversarial perturbation reveals fragility: if your model's decision flips when you slightly emphasize distractors, it's not trustworthy. By actively amplifying the hardest cases during training, the predictor learns to distinguish confident decisions from lucky ones. The gradient information helps because it shows exactly where the model is vulnerable. Stability under pressure is a better measure of reliability than raw accuracy on clean data.
1061.po: The system correctly retrieves relevant moments when they exist and rejects queries when no matching moment is present, handling cases with semantically similar but irrelevant interference. It significantly improves practical robustness compared to systems that always assume relevance exists.

1062.bp: Recommender systems predict what users will like by modeling user-item relationships as a graph (users and items as nodes, interactions as edges). Graph neural networks excel at this because they can capture how one user's taste connects to another through shared items. However, these models struggle with the actual patterns: they can't express complex nonlinear preferences, they miss big-picture structure across the entire graph, and noise in user interactions tricks them.
1062.wh: Standard graph neural networks model primarily pairwise relationships—'this user liked this item'—which is limited. They can't capture that three users collectively prefer certain item combos in ways that wouldn't be obvious from pairs. They also tend to wash out global patterns by over-smoothing local neighborhoods. And when users accidentally click on junk, that noise propagates through the graph without being filtered.
1062.ap: The method (FHCL) uses two complementary approaches together. First, it applies Fourier Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (a type of neural function decomposer) to disentangle complex user-item preference patterns into simpler pieces, then reconstructs the graph structure using a generative model (VGAE), capturing global information while discarding noise. Second, it creates a denoising view by selectively removing noisy edges and then checks how similar the denoised graph is to the original structure. These two views are compared using contrastive learning—the model learns to make them agree when they're both looking at the same good patterns, and disagree when one captures noise the other doesn't.
1062.ww: Decomposing interactions via Fourier KAN works because complex user preferences often hide simpler underlying components—factorization reveals them. Reconstructing through VGAE works because it forces the model to encode global structure, not just local edges. The contrastive framework works because comparing a clean view against a noisy view lets the model learn what robust patterns look like without explicit noise labels—agreement means the signal is strong enough to persist despite denoising.
1062.po: On recommendation benchmarks, this approach significantly outperforms prior graph neural network methods. It delivers more accurate predictions by simultaneously improving the model's nonlinear expressiveness, incorporating global structure, and building robustness against noisy interactions.

1063.bp: Educational videos (lectures, tutorials, demonstrations) contain diagrams, formulas, and visual explanations that are critical to answering questions correctly, yet large vision-language models often overlook these key visuals and instead focus on generic distractors (backgrounds, text labels). When a model answers 'what does this diagram show?' wrong, it's usually because it paid attention to the wrong region, not because it can't understand diagrams.
1063.wh: Vision-language models encode an image into features, and during generation, certain task-critical regions (a labeled diagram) end up with weaker feature signals than distractors (bright colors, prominent text). This isn't a training problem; it's a fundamental encoding-decoding mismatch. Simply training on more examples doesn't fix it because the model's attention during generation is already committed to ignoring weak signals.
1063.ap: The method (BAEI) intervenes during response generation without retraining the model. A lightweight neural network watches the model's internal attention patterns and predicts which candidate evidence regions (detected diagrams or key visuals) should be boosted, and by how much. It operates at two levels: in earlier layers, it cranks up the contribution of evidence signals; in later layers, it monitors prediction uncertainty and if confidence is shaky, it applies adaptive corrections. The policy network itself is trained via reinforcement learning (GRPO) to maximize final answer accuracy.
1063.ww: Intervening at decoding time works because the visual encoding is frozen but attention weights are plastic—boosting signals during generation rebalances where the model looks without full retraining. Operating at two levels works because early layers build representations and late layers make final decisions; tuning both provides coarse and fine control. GRPO training works because it optimizes directly for downstream performance without requiring manual annotation of which regions are evidence.
1063.po: On educational video QA benchmarks, the system significantly improves factual correctness by ensuring task-critical visual evidence receives appropriate attention. The model's backbone remains frozen, so the intervention is plug-and-play, and the approach generalizes across different educational datasets.

1064.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems answer questions by finding documents and reading them to construct answers. They work well when factual questions have clear, objective answers. But they fail in realistic decision-making scenarios where people have biases—asking for advice while harboring false beliefs, seeking confirmation rather than truth. The system then retrieves documents that confirm the bias, and the hallucination becomes worse, not better.
1064.wh: Standard RAG ranks documents by semantic relevance: 'Does this document match my query?' But when a query contains a false premise ('AI is definitely stealing all jobs'), relevant documents about AI actually reinforce the error. The real problem is treating relevance as a proxy for usefulness—they're not the same in biased decision-making. We need to know whether a document has enough evidential strength to steer someone toward correctness *despite* their bias.
1064.ap: The system (CoRM-RAG) uses causal reasoning to handle bias. During training, it synthetically creates user biases by perturbing queries (adding false premises, confirming biases, introducing logical fallacies). It learns to identify documents that are strong enough to correct these biased framings—documents with conflicting but authoritative evidence. This knowledge is distilled into a lightweight Evidence Critic that scores whether a document can actually guide a biased reasoning process toward correctness. The critic is then used during deployment to select retrieved documents.
1064.ww: Creating synthetic biases during training works because you can learn what 'strong enough evidence' looks like by observing which documents reliably correct various biases. The Evidence Critic works because it learns to value documents not by relevance but by corrective power—a document might not perfectly match the query but if it contains authoritative counter-evidence, it's more valuable. This aligns retrieval with decision safety rather than similarity.
1064.po: On decision-making benchmarks with adversarially biased queries, the system retrieves documents that steer the model toward correct answers despite cognitive biases, significantly outperforming standard dense retrievers. It also enables 'robustness scoring'—the model can abstain from answering when it detects insufficient evidence to overcome a query's bias, improving reliability.
